title: Ruth and Naomi
text:
During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech of Bethlehem took his wife Naomi and their two sons to the land of Moab. There the sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then Elimelech died, and about ten years later both sons died too. Naomi was left with no husband and no children, only two foreign daughters-in-law.

When she heard that there was food again in Judah, she set out for home and urged the young women to go back to their mothers' houses and find new husbands. Orpah kissed her and went. But Ruth clung to her. "Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried."

The two widows reached Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Ruth went out to glean the leftover grain behind the reapers, and by chance came to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. He had heard of her loyalty to Naomi and told his workers to let extra grain fall for her.

Guided by Naomi, Ruth asked Boaz to act as the family redeemer. He did so properly before the elders at the town gate, and married her. They had a son, Obed, and the women of Bethlehem placed the baby in Naomi's lap, saying that Ruth was better to her than seven sons. Obed became the grandfather of King David.
lesson: Family can be made by loyalty as well as by blood. Standing by an in-law in hard times can create bonds as deep as any.
date: ancient Israelite tradition (period of the judges)
